review_text: We really enjoyed our visit to the Turtle Hatchery in Hikkaduwa! It was both educational and heartwarming to see the conservation work being done to protect these incredible creatures. The staff were knowledgeable and passionate, taking the time to explain the different turtle species, their life cycles, and the challenges they face in the wild. Seeing the baby turtles and learning about the efforts to give them the best possible start was a highlight of our trip. It’s a great experience for all ages — informative, inspiring, and a nice way to support local wildlife conservation. Highly recommend stopping by if you’re in Hikkaduwa!

Visiting the Turtle Hatchery in Hikkaduwa was both an educational and heartwarming experience. The small facility is home to several species of sea turtles, many of which are rescued from injuries or hatched safely away from predators. It was wonderful to see the conservation efforts being made to protect these endangered creatures. The staff were friendly, informative, and clearly passionate about their work. They explained the different types of turtles, how they are cared for, and the steps taken to release them safely back into the ocean. You can even see baby turtles up close, and if you visit during the right time, you might get a chance to release them into the sea an unforgettable experience! The entry fee was very reasonable (around 500–1000 LKR), and it helps support the hatchery's ongoing efforts. Donations are also welcome. We spent about 45 minutes to an hour there. It’s not a large place, but every moment was engaging.The atmosphere was peaceful and humble. It’s not a flashy tourist spot, but it feels genuine and meaningful. It wasn’t too crowded when we visited (mid-morning), which made the experience more enjoyable and allowed time to interact with the staff.Extremely kind and knowledgeable. They patiently answered all our questions and clearly love what they do. Families, animal lovers, kids, and anyone interested in marine conservation. Highly recommend making a quick stop here if you’re in Hikkaduwa especially if you want your visit to make a positive impact.

We visited the Turtle Hatchery in Hikkaduwa during our stay at the Kalutara Royal Palms, and it was an experience of two very distinct halves. Let's start with the negative, which was entirely related to the journey. We decided to take a tuk tuk from Kalutara, which in hindsight was not a good idea. The distance is much longer than we anticipated, and the ride was hot, noisy, and quite uncomfortable for such a long trip. It took a significant chunk out of our day and was not the pleasant, scenic ride we had imagined. I would not recommend this mode of transport for this particular trip; hiring a private car would be a much better and safer investment for comfort and time. However, the Turtle Hatchery itself was absolutely amazing and completely worth the hassle of getting there. The work they are doing is truly inspirational. Seeing the tiny hatchlings and the larger rescued turtles up close was a heartwarming experience. The staff was passionate and knowledgeable, explaining the different turtle species, the threats they face, and the hatchery's conservation efforts. It felt good to know that our entry fee was contributing to a worthy cause. It's a truly educational and memorable visit, especially for families. The Turtle Hatchery in Hikkaduwa is a 5-star attraction. The journey from Kalutara in a tuk-tuk, however, was a 2-star experience. If you plan your transportation wisely, you are in for a fantastic and rewarding visit. We left with a little bit of dissatisfaction about the trip but with huge admiration for the hatchery itself.

During our tour with Hai Sri Lanka Tours, we were presented with the luxury of a visit to Hikkaduwa Turtle Hatchery, and it was one of the most spiritually enriching experiences along the entire trip. The hatchery is working a miracle to preserve sea turtles from taking care of turtles that were injured to safely incubating eggs and releasing the babies into the ocean. We got to see different species of turtles up close, learn about their life cycle, and even handle the adorable baby turtles (with care, of course!). It was informative and heartwarming to see the level of love and commitment that goes into conservation of Sri Lanka's wildlife. A big thank you to Hai Sri Lanka Tours for including this trip on our tour. Otherwise, we would not have found this wonderful experience. If you are visiting Sri Lanka, I strongly encourage you to visit the turtle hatchery especially with a caring and responsible tour company like Hai Sri Lanka Tours!

Welcome to Hikkaduwa, Sri Lanka, a breathtaking coastal haven where majestic sea turtles are not just visitors, but cherished residents. Hikkaduwa's vibrant coral reefs and protected beaches create a sanctuary for endangered sea turtles, including the graceful Green Turtle, the stunning Hawksbill with its serrated shell, and the colossal Leatherback. This is one of the best places on earth to witness these gentle giants up close! Why Hikkaduwa is Unmissable for Turtle Lovers Snorkel & Swim Alongside Them Glide through crystal-clear waters right off the beach and find yourself face-to-face with turtles peacefully grazing on seagrass or coral. An unforgettable, magical encounter! Witness Nature's Miracle (Seasonal) From May to October, join guided, responsible night walks (use only red light!) to observe massive females laboriously laying eggs on moonlit sands. Or, time your visit to marvel at tiny, determined hatchlings scampering towards the sea at dawn! Conservation in Action Visit renowned sanctuaries like the Sea Turtle Hatchery, where dedicated teams protect vulnerable nests, care for injured turtles, and release thousands of hatchlings – a truly heartwarming experience. Accessible Wonder Easily accessible from the main beach road, these encounters often happen just meters from shore, perfect for all ages and abilities. Experience the Wonder Responsibly Always maintain a respectful distance, never touch or chase the turtles, avoid flash photography, and support ethical sanctuaries. Hikkaduwa offers more than stunning beaches, it’s a front-row seat to the awe-inspiring world of endangered sea turtles. Come, create a memory that will glide through your heart forever! During our recent trip to Hikkaduwa, we visited the Turtle Hatchery, and it turned out to be one of the most meaningful and educational stops on our itinerary. While it's a small-scale operation, it's run with so much care, passion, and integrity by the owner and his family—you immediately feel the authenticity of their mission. Since we were visiting during the off-season, the hatchery was quiet and we had the entire place to ourselves. Although there weren’t many baby turtles being released that day, we were still able to see several species and sizes of turtles, each with their own rescue or rehabilitation story. It was a rare opportunity to engage up close and at our own pace. The owner, along with his wife and son, personally takes care of the turtles and runs the hatchery. Another kind gentleman assists with cleaning and maintaining the tanks. What stood out the most was the owner's deep knowledge and genuine dedication to protecting these endangered creatures. He spoke excellent English, patiently answering all our questions and explaining in detail how they locate turtle eggs, how the hatching process is monitored, and how the baby turtles are released at night to avoid predators like birds. You can tell this is not a commercialized setup, but a labor of love focused on conservation and education. We spent well over an hour here learning about the life cycle of sea turtles, their threats, and how even small operations like this are making a big difference. The hatchery is also conveniently located—just an easy tuk-tuk ride from the main Hikkaduwa beach stretch, making it a perfect short excursion if you're looking to do something meaningful and relaxed. A few tips: --Don’t expect a flashy or large-scale facility—this is a grassroots, family-run project with real heart. --Ask questions—the owner is incredibly knowledgeable and willing to share. --Bring some cash as your entry fee/donation helps sustain the hatchery's efforts.

This was an incredibly nice experience. We were greeted by very many friendly people who worked at the center. We paid an entrance fee of 2000 LKR per person and we did it gladly. The man who run the center (forgive us, but we do not remember his name), gave us a thorough tour and told us everything from how they buy turtle eggs from people who try to sell them to individuals, to when the turtles are released into the ocean. Our visit to the Turtle Hatchery Hikkaduwa was a truly remarkable and heartwarming experience that I highly recommend to anyone traveling in the area. From the moment we arrived, we were greeted by knowledgeable staff who were clearly passionate about their work and eager to share their expertise on sea turtle conservation. The highlight of our visit was the incredible opportunity to participate in releasing baby turtles back into the wild. It was not only educational but also an emotionally moving experience to see these tiny creatures start their journey into the ocean. The staff's dedication to the conservation of these beautiful animals was evident throughout our visit. the negative reviews i have read bewilder me and show a complete lack of understanding they survive on donation only, no entry fee and no government support. the bigger turtles wouldn't survive in the ocean due to ailments! They should be in bigger ponds then give them the $ to do so. Spending 2 hours at Turtle Hatchery Hikkaduwa was enlightening and inspiring. They are cared for by vets who visit every week.  That said, I think they could perhaps create a nicer environment, bigger tanks etc.  We were also surprised that they allowed visitors to touch/poke the turtles. Our guide was excellent and we did learn a lot. Considering the issues these beautiful creatures are having with swallowed plastic, one would think Sri Lanka should take note of their over use of the material - one of the worst countries we have visited in terms of caring for the environment. Lastly, the entry fee of 25 USD pp is a touch high but if it all goes into care and research, fair enough.

Entrance is 1000 Sri Lankan rupees, all funds, according to the owners, go to the maintenance, treatment, feeding of turtles and ransoming them from poachers. We took pictures of them and recorded a video as a souvenir) we held each one and stroked the big ones) We didn’t regret visiting, we recommend it 👍🏻

First of all, don't listen to all the negative reviews. I was a bit skeptical before going, but I loved every second of it. To all the eco-warriors bashing this place, the big rescue turtles here are disabled. They won't survive a day in the ocean. Thanks to conservation centers like this, they get to live longer. Have some common sense before posting negative reviews. It cost us Rs. 2000 per person for entry. This center is small, with multiple tanks and a sand pit where they keep the eggs. When we visited, there was a day-old baby turtle and a lot of 2-month-old turtles. They asked us to clean our hands before touching the turtles. The owner explained about the different types of turtles and where each turtle came to his center. We were fortunate enough to feed them fresh fish. It was a great experience. They release turtles within a month if they fully recover from injuries. However, if the turtles are permanently disabled, they keep them in the center. Location-wise, this place is extremely convenient as it is a 5-minute drive from the snorkeling area of Hikkaduwa.

People do everything they can to rescue injured turtles, patch them up and return them to the sea. Due to fishing, many turtles end up in nets and then lose a leg. Many turtles also get hooks in their mouths or eat plastic because they confuse it with jellyfish. The turtles are operated on, given antibiotics and even an "artificial statue" if possible. Eggs and baby turtles are protected and released into the sea.

This is a conservatory for turtles: the primary objective seems to be caring for wounded turtles and providing a safe environment for birth. The manager told us that they pay fishermen if they find any wounded/in-distress turtle and also if they bring eggs. All the eggs received are placed under sand with a tentative date of birth. We were told that the probability of birth goes from 5% to 80% under their care as the eggs are shielded from nature and predators. They have three/four types of turtles that they care for, and ultimately release into the sea. They also have several wounded turtles, some that will stay with them forever either because of permanent injury/disability or being endangered (there's a albino turtle). Overall, they are doing a terrific job at conserving turtles and it makes for a very enriching visit.

Amazing conservation experience, was wonderful to be able to hold baby turtles and release them into the ocean - so cute!! Definitely a cause worth supporting, and especially good to support them now that they are open after covid! Will definitely come back next time I visit Sri Lanka!

It turned out to be a good informative visit. These wild turtles are kept in this so called sanctuary for the entertainment of tourists and profit.  All these turtles should be set free but they are not? Five of us, three adults and two kids, visited the turtle farm at Hikkaduwa.  Foreigners are charged an entry fee of Rs 500. The current owner’s father had started the farm in 2000.  After he died later that year his sister and the rest of the family had taken over the farm.  All his family - his mother, two sisters and their children had all perished during the tsunami on 26th December 2004.  We visited the hatchery on 26th December 2019, exactly fifteen years after the tsunami.  The owner and his brother were the only survivors as they were working in Colombo.  The current owner then rebuilt this farm from scratch and opened it to conserve the turtle population. At night, adult turtles dig a hole at the beach and lay their eggs within.  Some people collect these eggs at night.  Eggs have a thriving market at some people believe that turtle eggs make them strong and tough.  The owner buys them from villagers by paying a premium price.  They are then buried in sand with up to 100 eggs in each mound and incubated for about 48 days.  Once the eggs hatch, they are released back into the ocean.  We were told that the survival rate of the baby turtles is only one in hundred, others falling prey while in the sea! These turtles, these huge marine reptiles who survive, migrate and move to far distant places in the sea.  However, they remember to return to the exact spot where they were born to mate and lay their own eggs and the cycle continues.  There are many places in Sri Lankan beaches where turtles return to lay eggs. Turtles were kept in eight tanks, measuring about 3m x 2m. In there we saw some infirm and injured turtles being taken care of.  Some were sans flippers and others with injured hind legs.  We were told that turtles are injured at sea, getting caught in fishing nets.  Others are injured when humans try to catch them for meat!  Here, at this turtle farm they attempt to revive and heal them to full recovery before releasing them back into the ocean.  There is a billboard requesting visitors to not touch the turtles. A laudable great conservation effort!

We were reluctant to go initially after seeing several bad reviews, however glad we bit of bullet and went anyway. Clearly those who wrote the bad reviews hadn’t actually spoken to the gentle who owned this place, we did: When turtles loose a limb at sea (e.g. by the propeller of a boat) they then don’t know how to dive and just float atop the tea. They eventually often wash up ashore somewhere, if a local finds one and they bring it to this gentleman he pays them a fair price for the turtle. He then teaches the to dive using its 3 remaining limbs by keeping them in water of different depths, until eventually it learns. When we were there we could see the progression as he had some that could only float atop the water, and others who were sitting on the bottom. After they learn to dive again he releases them back into the wild. He also told us how the locals will steal the turtle eggs which get laid on the beach to sell as food, he buys them off these locals (for 4 times the going rate) and hatches then himself. I went there with another person and in total we found 3 dead turtle babies in the pool! No one noticed they were dead! I mean wtf? You should think about what you are doing guys! This is not good. Also no one is watching the visitors! So people just lift up the turtles and no one cares .... this is not acceptable! You have maybe good thoughts but its a very bad implementation! Als wir 500Rs Eintritt gezahlt haben, sind wir direkt zu den Becken mit den Schildkröten gelaufen. Allerdings hat uns niemand begleitet und uns hat auch niemand was über die Schildkröten erklärt. Die Becken sind echt winzig und die Schildkröten haben nicht viel Freiraum. Ich habe ein paar Fragen zu den kranken Tieren gestellt, um zu wissen warum sie hier sind und was mit ihnen passieren wird. Allerdings konnte keiner wirklich so gut englisch und somit haben sich meine Fragen erübrigt. Das geht gar nicht! Mindestens eine Person sollte etwas auf englisch über die Geschichte der jeweiligen Schildkröten erzählen können. Was bringt es mir, sorry, halb leblose traurige Schildkröten in winzigen Becken anzustarren ohne das ich weiß warum?? Außerdem hat niemand die BEsucher wirklich beobachtet und somit haben einige einfach die Schildkröten raus gehoben und es hat niemanden interessiert. Nope, geht gar nicht! Guter Gedanke, aber schlechte Umsetzung.
This over priced turtle hatchery is not worth it. You'll find nothing interesting here. Toi small a place. And 1000 lkr, almost 400 indian rupees.

We visited this place with no expectations. We were amazed to hear the story of the sea turtles. The guide provided us with a lot of information regarding the roll of the sea turtles savers in a clear and understandable way. I wish they wouldn’t let anyone touch the turtles (they know they shouldn’t but sometimes tourists mistakenly thinks it’s cute and the locals don’t stop them). Overall it’s a small yet an interesting place to visit.

A simple place that doesn’t take too long to go around. Lots of varieties of turtles to see, many have been injured by fishermen and brought to either recover before releasing or to stay their if they wouldn’t survive in the ocean The eggs are dated and the hatchlings put into two tanks   One day olds and two day olds. The turtles are released on their second day which you can do for an extra 1000 rupees We all chose our baby turtle and walked down to the beach and released them one by one. A wonderful experience

On arrival, I was greeted by a member of staff. I asked how much it would be and what would be included. He said 500 rupees. He asked for how many people, I said 1. I have him 1000 rupees and then he tried to give me 2 tickets and take payment and I had to say firmly that it was only for me and to give me change. This was not a nice greeting. On proceeding in there was a man shouting loudly about the different turtles and trying to give some kind of talk about the turtles. It felt very rehearsed and he repeated himself several times, to which point I took myself off to look at the turtles. There was little interaction as a group as the man could only be heard raising his voice and sounding quite harsh. They seem to be doing some good work to rescue turtles that have been injured from propellors of boats or are unwell so that they can be returned to their natural habitat. I question how effective the tour is as it did little to educate me. I learnt more from the posters on the walls and I did take some lovely photographs. It's worth a visit but don't expect to stay there for long - I'd say 30 minutes at the most. Be careful of the staff on entry!

20 minutes is enough time to spend here.   They are doing great conservation work here and the turtle are nice to look.  It is about 10 mins tuk tuk from Hikkaduwa alongside the Tsunami museum on monuments.
It is nice that u can give experience to the kids to hold the small turtles and see different sizes. But it is very small place and u can only see few of them

Kids liked the visit which lasted 10 minutes. I was not impressed. The place totally missed to express any love towards the animals, nor energy into welcoming people other than taking their 500 rupies.

When we first arrive it was Nice, me and boyfriend just walked around and looked at The beautiful creatures. But after a while a group Of Girls came in and The guy that worked there said that they could pick up The turtels... And they did. They played around with them like they where toys. So sad to see.. And one Of The Girls drop a little one on The floor... Dont go there

Good place if you have tiny travelers with you. They charge you Srinlankan Rupees 1000/- for an entry and another 500/- if you want to release a baby turtle back to sea. They will explain you everything about turtles and various species. However, these farms are not Govt Maintained, looks more like a promotional activity.

My rating is based upon the condition of the adult turtles, and I do not wish to discredit the big efforts being made to save the baby turtles by the Hatchery. It is great that this work is being done to protect the eggs and make sure the baby turtles get a fighting chance. However, visiting the Hatchery made us feel very uncomfortable. The adult turtles were kept in very small basins without anything to distract or inspire them, and one of them kept biting the side of the basin. We were told they would be kept in the basin for 1.5 years for educational purposes and to show to tourists, and then released. 1.5 years is a long time for a turtle to live under such circumstances, and if it hasn't lost its mind by then, how will it survive in the wild after so long in captivity? There was an albino turtle, which I am assuming would never be released. It was very sad to see the injured turtles - they seemed to have lost all spark, and were mostly not even moving. The guide that showed us around did so very quickly and he was hard to understand, and he quickly returned to the little office. I felt that I left with far more questions than when I arrived, and I wish that the adult turtles could be given a little more space!
Good place for kids to learn on turtle life and understand more depth about turtles. Not just a place for kids but even for adults to find out more
We stopped on our way to Colombo and it was very nice to see tiny turtles swim around. A must see place.

Based a little out of town, it’s a very small hatchery and you honestly don’t need more than 10 minutes there. We were the only ones there on a rainy day and the tour was informative but very quick, considering the entrance price. Guess they can’t rely solely on donations - hope it does actually go where it should. Also have mixed feelings on picking up baby turtles, each to their own.

While I do not doubt the good work being done here, I do doubt if it is worth a visit. We went on a quiet day. Staff were very quick to collect our Rs 500 p/p entry fee but then dissapeared. No one bothered to guide us or explain what they do. It is also really small and you can literally see everything in less than 10 minutes.

The baby turtles are super cute, and you're allowed to hold them... But most of the larger turtles are rescued so have missing limbs which is so sad to see. The organiser also has a sad story about the 2004 Tsunami so you should visit to help him to help the turtles.

We’d been recommended this by a local. Small hatchery with tanks housing new borns to injured old turtles... these turtles are given care & rehabilitated until strong enough to be released. It’s a shame these places need to exist but it’s great that there are kind ppl like the owner who dedicate their lives to saving this vulnerable species.

an amazing place that does amazing work!! after visiting the elephant orphanage, i had lost hope for what to expect here, however i was pleasantly surprised. our guide had so much love for these turtles and there was no questions he couldn’t answer. he showed us how they wait for the eggs to hatch, the baby turtles that they keep for 3 days until they’re strong enough to be released and the poorly turtles in the ‘hospital’ tanks. we got to release our own turtles into the ocean which is so heartwarming and once in a lifetime. this hatchery has helped over 4 million turtles and i hope they can continue this amazing work!!

The Turtle Hatchery is a basic facility highlighting the need for protection of turtles of all kinds in the coastal regions of Sri Lanka. There is a small area set aside for egg protection & hatching with around 12 tanks housing injured, juvenile and local species. You are able to handle the juvenile turtles but not the adults as they can injure you with their quite sharp beaks. The entry fee is minimal but so is the presentation of the Hatchery. This does not, however, diminish the great effort to conserve and preserve this wonderful sea creature in danger of being lost to predators both animal & plastic!

This place conserves the turtles that are injured in the ocean. The turtles that come & lay eggs here are then released in the ocean close to sunset time. This place is not government aided so people who visit can put in some amount of donation post the guided tour. Loved to catch the 1 day old as well as older turtles in hand. Kids will enjoy.
We stopped on our way from Galle to Hikkaduwa. Very worth while stop and your ticket helps with the conservation work.
So nice to visit a place working so seriously with conservation of turtles 😊 Good information from the guide, he did very well 😎 Really worth a visit 👍

These are private setup where people volunteer to conserve any stray, injured or endangered turtles. They feed them till they are old enough to survive on their own. They completely take care of the injured turtles till the last breath.

We were so impressed by the work which is being carried out at this turtle sanctuary. It is so important and everyone needs to visit to not only visit , but to help promote its importance. It was quite extraordinary being able to actually touch these amazing creatures who are so under threat.
We were glad to visit this place! You can pet the turtles! And get a lot of knowledge about them. Very cool for kids!

This was incredibly special. Thank you to our guide around the sanctuary (wish I'd gotten his name) he was beaming with passion for his job! Very informative & such great work is being done with these babies. They also show so much care for their disabled turtles who wouldn't survive in the wild. There is also an albino turtle whose name is Michael Jackson (who wouldn't survive in the wild without camouflage) was the star of the show! Thanks guys!

After seeing it so high on the to do list in Hikkaduwa we went along and found it to be a let down and kind of sad to see the large turtles in small pools. I wish the people working there would give you a bit of information on them and their rehabilitation. I understand if you see the young ones being released it would leave a smile on the dial.

Pay 500 each to get in and it’s not a happy experience. One lady ahead of us lifted a baby out of the tank which was obviously dead. The older turtles swim in circles hitting the sides attempting to get out. The tanks are plain concrete with nothing for the animals but water. I feel it is more of a money making enterprise than something with the turtles as the highest priority.

We spent less than 5 minutes here. Having paid 500 each at the entrance, the staff returned straight to the office and went on their phones, there was no tour or information other than the very dated info boards. The eggs are taken directly from the beach, supposedly to stop locals eating them. The small turtles had plenty of space, but there were only about 5 in the tank. There were many large turtles that were 1/4 the size of their enclosure. Many turtles were biting the side of the concrete walls and trying to climb out. Some turtle shells were covered in algae due to filthy water and no room to move. Overall there was no sign of rehabilitation to the wild here, more so people trying to make money off the back of animals suffering in captivity.

500lkr entry fee - we got a talk for around 5 minutes on the 3 different type of turtle they had there and the effects of humans/pollution has on them and how big they can get l. There is maybe 10 tanks all very small which is fine for the hatchlings but some of the bigger ones had hardly any room to move. There were some in rehab from injuries. Hopefully the 500 is well spent and is actually all for releasing them back into the wild like they said. Only they will know if this is genuine though.

Every time i visit Sri Lanka, I make sure i come here. To hold the turtles and interact with them up close is an unique experience which one should not miss.. Also commendable is the way they protect these creatures who come here to lay eggs. A small entry fees is entirely ok to visit such an amazing place

My wife and I visited the Kagoolga Turtle Hatchery- it was a special experience and we loved it. I think if you can do-ordinate a time when they release the turtles to the ocean that is when it is best to go- unfortunately our timing did not allow that to happen. This activity was organised by Blue Lanka tours and I’m thankful they did- it was a nice stop over on the way to Galle and the volunteer who took us through the hatchery and explained everything to us and of course introduced us to the injured and baby turtles was a once in a lifetime experience. I was a little confused as we were asked to tip the guide and there was also a donation box at the door when we were leaving so wasn’t sure if we had to donate as well as tip/ donate the volunteer. But brilliant 30 minute stop over- highly recommend this as a time filler but as I said time it so you can see the baby turtle release on the beach

Stopped here on the way down south. So interesting to hear the information about the turtles and great to see how they look after the injured turtles. There were a number of little baby turtles that we all loved, especially our two year old great nephew, who was so excited by being able to see and touch them.  Half of our group had been indifferent about stopping at the hatchery but all agreed afterwards that it was a highlight. Definitely a cause worth supporting as they do important work maintaining the population of turtles in the world.

We were lucky enough to visit the hatchery and see the work being carried out there. Beautiful little hatchlings and larger Green Turtles and Oliver Ridley turtles. Some injured turtles also being cared for. We happily paid the 500 rupee admission.

There wasn’t a whole lot going on in Hikkaduwa when we visited off season, so we took a walk up to the turtle hatchery from our villa. Entry was 500r each and the blokes just sat in the doorway reading the newspaper. They left us to look around at the turtles, telling us how they buy and bury eggs from people who illegally steal them, as well as how they help injured turtles etc. To be honest, you can see everything in 15 minutes. There’s 12 or 13 turtles, some are asleep and some look distressed just swimming into the side of their pool. I want to think what they tell you is true but I have my doubts - particularly because further down the road in Galle there’s another hatchery place, so I wonder how much conservation happens. You can also hold the baby turtles for Instagram pics, which feels a bit odd for a conservation place. Needless to say, we didn’t. Would I go again? There’s not a lot to do in off season in Hikkaduwa - especially when raining! If I was in the area I’d be interested to go in and see if they have changed turtles. Value for money? It doesn’t take long to look round but you see turtles! And you are supposedly helping with your entry fee so all good from me!

Well worth the visit, the owner clearly cares passionately about the survival of the turtles. Good explanation of all the different types of turtles in the hatchery and how he cares for them and rehabilitates the injured. Definitely recommend if you are in the area and have a spare hour

Only takes 15 minutes but we’ll worth the entry fee - proceeds help conservation of turtles. Can pick up turtle hatchlings. Saturday evening at 5pm they release the hatchlings on the beach so if you can, visit around then

An amazing experience and these guys are doing an incredible thing trying to educate locals and save the sea turtles. The center had a few large, injured sea turtles, in small-ish tanks, however when we asked about this the guys said that they were being rehabilitated and learning to dive again after their injury, and showed us the turtles that are almost ready to be released back to the sea. The guys alsO rescue turtle eggs, and once hatched they release them into the sea. This is a family run conservation center and the guys were so knowledgable- however you do have to ask questions as there are not many posters etc. We particularly like that the guys explained that they charge tourists, however they do not charge locals, as they want to educate the local people to help them to understand the importance of sea life conservation- brilliant!!! We 100000% recommend you visit this place, and help to save the sea turtles of Sri Lanka.
Nothing much more to visit but worth to stop by if ur traveling through hikkaduwa,coz it's only few minutes watch....

It's just a small place with a few tanks for the different turtles. They will tell you about the different types of turtle and have one of each to show you, which they keep for a certain length of time before releasing them. There were lots of hatchlings ready to be released, which you were allowed to hold, and we spent some time on the beach out the back while we waited for release time. They also had some injured turtles, but they didn't seem to have much space considering their size. They didn't really educate people about releasing them, so some people were putting cameras between the turtles and the sea, which made it harder for the hatchlings to make it to the sea.

Visited Turtle Hatchery on a rainy day. Hopefully the money (500) is well spend. It is really small and after a few minutes and photos you’re done. Unfortunately no explanation about the purpose and vision of this hatchery.
Really worth a visit I made friends with the turtles no more plastic now for me. They run the turle hatchery on donations and you can see they are well cared for

We went from Hikkaduwa, it is very close and easy to get to in a tuktuk. It is a small place but has lovely turtles that you can touch and pick up. They do a great job. It is good value at 500 rupees per person.

You cant come away from this place without being genuinely touched  by how man kind and all the plastic we use is destroying the beauties of the world. The sanctuary is small but the talk they give and being able to touch and see the turtles makes this a definite place to visit while your in Hikkaduwa.

We all learned something today at the hatchery and it was certainly worth it. I'm glad we came. There is a good educational effort on behalf of the hatchery and they help rescue and release turtles back into the wild that have been hurt. A good activity close to the tsunami photo museum. Defiantly do both if in hikkudawa.
A Nice little place to visit. I really like that the turtles Seem to thrive. Worth a visit, and easy to get there by bus from hikkaduwa

The have a large number of turtles being hatched regularly and they release them in the night due to eagles and other birds of prey. Its an amazing project and a big thank you to the people who donate regularly to keep the place running and to the volunteers. They have different species and even handicap. Very touched by the good work on going to save the species.

We were totally humbled by the great work this not for profit hatchery undertakes purely though the foreign and local visitor donations.  It is amazing to hear the 1 to 5 ratio of success rate compared to the 1 to 1000 in the wild. If not for these types of organisations, these endangered turtle species will most certainly be wiped out.

A small place, little pools for the turtles, a quick speech from someone about saving the turtles. Can’t say if that’s true or not, I hope it is but the turtles don’t benefit from you visiting.. very sad!
Must visit to see how pollution plastics and other debris is affecting the sea animals. Commendable works done by the persons working there
Really enjoyed seeing the baby turtles. The eggs are harvested and re buried in the sand and baby turtles released into the sea. Caring conservationists.

I spent almost 2 hrs there though it is a small hatchery but shows you entire liffe cycle of turtles from an egg to a turtle... Life time experience is to hold 1-2 days turtles in your hand!!! Very informative.. place needs more maintenance by the authorities but overall that's an amazing experience..
Very emotional visit. Sad to see what is happening to the turtles Very happy to see someone care about this situation
Good deal of varieties of turtles and associated info, although the pools could be better maintained. Gift shop in a somewhat opportunistic mode at the time of our visit.
Foundation by Local Family for the Turtle Hatchery Saving Them from Extinction, Feel them on your Hands.

It costs LKR500 for a ticket to the hatchery, not much in USD, but relatively speaking a lot. The Tsunami Museum nearby, which is well worth a visit, is by donation. If you are glad to see maimed turtles alive, nurtured and swimming alone in small tanks, and if you or your children will enjoy picking up the baby turtles, do go. If not, give it a miss, and make a larger donation to the Tsunami Museum.
We visited the hatchery during the off season. We could pick up baby turtles and participated in setting approx. 30 turtles into the sea during our visit. Great experience and recommendable

It was great experience to watch sea turtles at hikkaduwa. You must visit this place if you travel in sri lanka. You may visit lots of baby turtles and can get all information about thire life circle.
500 Rupees ti get in. Interesting instructive talk. You can touch the little ones. Additional donations welcome - they ate doing a good job actually.

If you are traveling with kids, this place just is so exciting and lovely experience. You can see baby turtles.. hold them in your hand and actually look at these rare gentle creatures.. They have a variety of species from one day old to 25 year old ones as well.. Very well maintained and hope they are genuine and real int he way they contribute to the living of this beautiful species...

We visited whilst in Hikkaduwa. We were greeted by the owner, who seemed very passionate and was very informative. I’ve read some pessimistic reviews and can only hope he is as genuine as he seemed. The entry price was 500 pp, so I cannot see this being a “for profit” company. There were many injured Turtles in 1.5m x 1.5m enclosure pools. I was told that they go through a period of rehabilitation i.e. teaching them to swim with missing limbs in shallower water until they are fit, before being released. There were eggs and also 4 day old hatchlings, which I was told would be released later that week on a beach a few hundred meters away. Everything seemed well and I hope that it is all as genuine as I was led to believe.

It was great to see how this conservation project works in practice, watching the new hatchlings emerge which we were able to release into the tanks where they spend a short time before going into the sea. We did not witness this because it was the wrong time of day, but you could request to visit at the right time I believe. It was very thought-provoking to see the damaged turtles which are being nurtured, unable to live in the wild but well taken care of here. There was a small shop with handicrafts on sale too. Everyone should visit.
Very sweet and nice place. You must pay to go in. A good cause so I would advise going. Very small hatchery.

This hatchery - even though very small was a highlight of our time in Hikkaduwa.  We were so lucky to be able to pick up the turtles and learn about them and the reason why this hatchery was established - well done to the owners who are following on from their fathers vision.  Definately worth a visit

A really well run and environmentally concious turtle sanctuary. Great to interact with newly hatched turtles and see injured animals rehabilitated. Staff were friendly and knowledgeable. Lucky enough to see a releasing of baby turtles but obviously not a guarentee and not to be expected.
This is a place you will know more about turtles, their lifespan, types etc. There are amazing stories of the rescued turtles and you can actually see and touch them.
Visited this place in the month of April, got a chance to release the baby turtles of 3 days old into sea, good place to know about turtle breeds.

This little hatchery in Hikkaduwa was on the beach, and we learned about the necessity of it from the owner. According to him, some Sri Lankans believe they get strength from eating sea turtle eggs. So what he does is buys them from the locals at a higher price, or finds them in the sand and relocates them to the hatchery before the locals get there. An interesting fact is that the sex of the turtle is determined by the temperature of the egg. So the turtles at the top of the pile, being the warmest, are female, and the ones at the bottom are male. Once the little turtles hatch, they are released into the ocean. This place also takes in disabled turtles that have lost flippers from shark attacks, or from fishermen’s nets. Here they are taught how to swim and dive again in a variety of pools with varying depths. Once they can fully maneuver properly, they too are released back to their natural habitat.

We were taken here by our driver. The owner showed us around and explained a bit about the process of getting the eggs and releasing the turtles, as well as rehabilitating the injured turtles. The kids loved seeing and holding the turtles. Hoping our donation will be used correctly. Also hoping people aren’t now digging up eggs knowing that the hatchery will buy them.

Visited early morning. A very small place indeed but it was warm friendly and informative. We didn't touch any of the turtles despite being allowed to. (Not squeamish at all,  but I like to leave nature alone). The guy running the place gave out plenty of info during his limited tour and then it was wander at leisure. We didn't take advantage of using our entry tickets to re-attend to see the hatchlings  being released into the sea in the evening (as we had seen this before elsewhere) For those who complain of the 500 LKR entrance fee, I can only say, that I think it is a small price to pay to help keep this worthwhile facility running.

These young men at this facility doing a wonderful job, doing there best to protect and release the turtles to the sea at the right time, this is small facility but well kept, very clean and they take a good care of the turtles who suffer due to to unethical fishing practices and some lost there wings/ flips as well. If your visiting with young kids it’s a lovely experience and if possible give a helping hand to this hatchery.

We stopped here for a short visit, but ended up spending almost an hour. As others have said, there are tanks with large and small turtles. You get a talk/tour from one of the managers, who'll explain the conservation aims and methods they use. Turtles who are 1-3 days old are released back to the sea in the evening, but we did not have time to wait till then. My kids were happy to hold the tiny babies, and to touch the larger ones. We did not see any one holding big turtles and neither did we want to. Perhaps we had to ask them, and then they'd let us. But we were happy with the small ones. There are some disabled turtle, hurt by boats and nets. These are trained gradually to learn how to float and swim without the full complement of flippers. When they are ready, these are released back to wild.

It's simply a dozen pools. One with loads of baby turtles, the other with larger ones that cannot be released. Costs 500 per person. There is a hatchery. They buy the eggs from locals to hatch to avoid people eating them. 500 rupees buys 100 eggs.

A small place held by a great people who dedicate their lives to help and to care for turtles found on the beaches, orphans or wildlife victims. The stuff is very informative, knowledgeable and obviously passionate about what they are doing. This place is all about education and building awareness. They really do care about these turtles and want to help them. Not only you can learn about their lifespan/environment and issues facing these creatures, but also be a part of this great experience and donate the institution or particular turtle. You and your kids simply gonna love it.

Spent and hour there with our 3 year old. We all thought it was a fantastic experience and exceptional value for money, I think it was Rs500 each (£2.25), with our daughter being free. We were shown around the facility and given an intro to the life of a turtle. The highlight for us was holding the one day old turtles, our 3 year old was in her element!!
A quaint little place, if you arrive at 5.15pm you can release a little turtle into the sea. Great host who does a good job of explaining everything.

This is a delight to visit. You get a guided overview tour and an understanding and viewing of many different Turtle breeds. You get to hold them and watch their varying stages of maturing. They hatch the eggs which have been saved and handed in by local  fisherman and when mature enough they are released back into their natural environment.  Not trashy or touristy, just simple, effective and dedicated. Small admission fee and opportunity to provide a donation if you wish.

Great wee trip. Its a must. Take tuk tuk just 10 min ride away. Staff vey informative. Its not a big place but really interesting. Releasing of the babies usually takes place around 5.30pm. Now that was awesome. Entry 500 ruoees per person.

Stolen eggs from turtles nests are bought, reburied, hatched and set free. An amazing cause. The owner lost his whole family to the tsunami and now does this. Hold one day old baby turtles. Tip: If you go around 5pm you can help set the baby turtles free into the ocean.

On a recent trip to Hikkaduwa, we had the opportunity to go to the turtle hatchery and conservation center.  The entrance fee was very reasonable (about 7 US dollars total for our whole family).  We learned about the different types of turtles, the life cycle of the turtles, and the threats to turtles in Sri Lanka.  Most importantly we learned about how the conservation center protects the animals.  We had the chance to see one, three, and five day old turtles.   You could hold the three day old turtles which very honesty moved me to tears they were so beautiful.  They also had turtles who would not make it in the wild that they care for and use to teach visitors.  It was a wonderful experience that I very highly recommend!

The whole sanctuary is literally 8 small basins with turtles in them. The adult ones have been hurt or are unable to survive in the wild. There are two basins with the babies. No supervision so you could pick them up to your hearts content. I’m no animal specialist but I imagine this can’t be good. At nightfall you can help release them in the water. In general, nothing special. We were done in 20 minutes.

In our way to tsunami museum we stop also at the Turtle Hartchery. The entrance fee was 1000 Rps (for the locals the price is less expensive). We had a guide that presented us the mini pools with the turtles, but he was not involved , repeating the speech as a poetry. You have a little time to make some pictures with the little turtles. Hope the fee is going for save the turtles not to attract tourist.

This is an amazing place all centred around education.   Don’t miss a trip here.   The owner is very knowledgeable and his efforts are commendable.   We were lucky enough to go on a day when some turtles had hatched and were able to return in the evening to help release them into the sea. Just lovely.

The first thing we were told was that only 2% of hatchlings are female, The fact is that left alone that figure would be 50/50.  As a result of this interference the turtles are doomed to be wiped out. Science tells us that turtle gender is dependent on the sand temperature and moisture content when the eggs are incubating. These aspects are not addressed in the so called sanctuary, no research or science at all. The nests are robbed and the hatchlings put on display for tourists to play with. Not to mention the appalling conditions in which the turtles are kept. Do not contribute to the destruction of these amazing animals.

The men that run this operation are truly magical! They rescue the turtle eggs from poachers, relay them in secure sand and then when they hatch, make sure that they are strong enough before they are released back into the sea. It is very educational with information about the different species and the devastating affects of humans on these beautiful creatures. Lovely to see the newly hatched turtles swimming around and playing with each other. You need no more than 30mins. We were invited back that evening at 5.30pm to release some of the turtles back into the sea, I'm sure this would have also been a wonderful experience, unfortunately we did not have time.

Located around 4 km distance from the main town this place consist of variety of tutles from the baby tutles to large older turtles. The experience is worth it as your allowed to touch and feel the baby turtles.However they should improve on the space and overall cleanthiness of the sourrounding in order to have a better display of the turtles

We visited last week,a must do while in Sri Lanka.Pretty sad to see the concrete tanks and the hatchlings swimming frantically,must be exhausted by the time they are released.What hope do they have?Creatures yanked from tanks for photos added to the dismal experience.Went home and did a literature search,no reputable marine body has a good thing to say,a good idea gone horribly wrong.So no.

500 slr fee with 10+ varieties of turtles. They give you some history and information on life cycle and life of turtles. You can spend half n hour to an hour depending on your interests. Dint find it very helpful.
This is one of the our fvt place in sri lanka, this place is awesome so cute baby turtle , and they take care of them very well, good friendly people in there ,

I have been to many turtle sanctuaries and this is one of the best with it easy to see 5 of the 7 species of turtle at different stages of growth. During hatching season There are babies you can hold them there are yearlings who are all on the way to be released plus older ones generally injured in open tanks. The staff are very helpful and tell you all about the turtles and what they are doing. It is fantastic for kids and adults alike - very reasonable to get in at 500 R but also do give a donation - they need all the help they can get!

we visited this hatchery on our return to bentota from galle. the manager anad guide was very well informed, gave us details on the 5 types ofturtles, the problems they face from humans, the health issues faced by hatchings.. albanian, blind, lame, and weak. the tour is 1 hour .. very informative and touchiing. outside is a store.. we bought stuff as the proceeds go towards the keeping of the turtles. highly recommend to all
Worth the visit or once if you have not visited. Nice to see different types of Turtle and Tortoise. There is a small price for ticket. You can take photos with the turtles.

Amazing collection of turtles, you will get to know them from birth to death....The owner takes care of them, feeds them and when they are healthy leaves them in the open waters..!! Worth a visit.....and a must do when in Hikkaduwa!!!

The people there were realy nice. They shaw as the place around and they gave us so many infomations about the turtles. We could touch the turtles and even hold them in our hands. Above all the money that you pay for the ticket goes for a good perpose, to preserve an animal speace
They are very passionate about their mission and that is marvelous. Visit if you can, donate if possible and we can enjoy seeing turtles in the beach many years to come.

If you wish to see several types of turtles in various age groups, even those who are of one day old, this is quite teh place to be. If you are a foreigner who travels in LK,  you should purchase a ticket, for Sri Lankans also the same, but quite a cheaper ticket. They provide you information of the turtles as well
The staff was very welcoming and their personal story is very touching related to the tragic moments of Tsunami. They save injured turtles and I feel honored to visit that place!
It's a really great visit, I learn a lot about turtles. The staff is really friendly and supportive. Great work...!!!

Amazing place to visit.  Very knowledgeable staff who speak an host of different languages.  Complete life cycle of a variety of turtle explained and questions answered.  You will get to see newly hatched babies just before release and many other older turtles of various ages and size that can't be released for different acceptable reasons such has injuries etc.  Even get to old the beautiful Monica

The owner of the hatchery gives everyone who enters his personal attention. He will walk you thru the egg nesting area and holding tanks explaining environmental issues, conservation and rescue issues. He will knowledgeably answer any questions you may have. 500 rupee to enter, stay as long as you like but an hour should suffice. His mission is not just to save and rehabilitate disabled turtles, buy back turtle eggs to prevent them being sold for human consumption, but to educate young people so that they support turtle conservation in the future.

They are helping small turtles to hatch safely and go to the sea when they are ready, Great work Only drawback is the lack of space for the more seriously injured that have to remain as they would not survive in the wild.

Very few species though. But good to see small and big, young and old turtles and even the turtle eggs at one place. We didn’t get to see any eggs hatching or any turtles to be set free in the sea. So don’t expect that to happen
A beautiful rehabilitation centre and hatchery that protects all species of sea turtles. So i happy we went here ❤️

I am always a bit suspicious when there's endangered animals and tourists at the same place. But I'm quite sure that this place is what they claim to be. It is a small place and with 500rs entry you get short information about turtles and to see the small and bigger turtles that they say they are going to release to the sea. I think there is a possibility to go with them to the beach and release small turtles to the sea, but that's only at certain times. Worth to visit!! And the TripAdvisor map is incorrect (6. March 2018). According to that the place should be in Colombo. It's not. But you find the place from google maps

It is really a great experience to learn about the turtles especially as their life span which on average for turtles can be around 180 years and in fact 300 years for some species. What is the secret of their longetivity ? It was inspiring to see the rehabilitation of injured turtles which lose their flippers to boat propellers and the breeding of young turtles from eggs collected from sea shores. Eggs are eaten be man and birds/animals alike and this hatchery gives more chance for the eggs to hatch. It was set up after the tsunami of 2004 and a very good effort by the local  family which has set this up....

Turtles are kept in really tiny empty concrete enclosures - it's cruel and I can't imagine how these creatures can be happy, yet alone comfortable. Guy quickly showed us around and it became obvious that they are just there to get your 500Rs entry fee. Guy reels off a blurb about how they release the adults every year or so with zero conviction. Lots of tourists picking the babies up and taking selfies. If you have any shred of care about the welfare of animals, do not contribute to this and make the same mistake we did. Animal tourism in one of its worst forms.

A brief stop as we travelled up the coast. Not a big fan of most animal based attractions but this was informative and enjoyable. After paying a modest entrance fee we were given the tour and an excellent explanation of the rescue and rehabilitation work carried out. Most of the adult Turtles have been injured at sea and they are usually released back after recuperating. They also hatch eggs which visitors can then put the hatchlings back into the ocean. Only criticism is the lack of space for the more seriously injured that have to remain as they would not survive in the wild.

The Turtle Hatchery is very small, not worth to pay 500Rupees to visit. There's a gentlemen showing us around is not friendly at all which is really a big turn off unlike all the other Sri Lankan people we had met.

It was very refreshing to see a group of people care that much about turtles of all species. They are very knowledgeable and will answer any questions you might have. You are able to gently hold the baby turtles and only observe the older rehabilitating turtles. They  assist in the long recovery of attacked or injured turtles by teaching them how to dive and surface again. Make sure to keep your ticket because you can return the evening of purchase to release to babies into the sea.

One of the staff showed us the different pools and gave detailed information about how they are helping to save the sea turtles. Was an experience to see the newly born sea turtles and the rehab of unfortunately injured adult turtles. We were lucky enough to see the new born turtles get released into the ocean too! I believe this hatchery is doing a fantastic job to protect and conserve the sea turtles. Not a tourist trap. They dont ask for much, just donations if you wish to help and a small entry fee.

Definitely worth visiting. The manager took us through the whole running of the hatchery and we even got to come back see the release of the newborn turtles of the day at 5.30pm - purely magical. He’s working for a great cause, saving hundreds of baby and adult turtles every year and educating the local community and visitors. His dad started this hatchery and sadly died in the tsunami in 2004 with almost the entire family. He rebuilt everything from nothing. Truely an inspiring man.

1. I liked the fact that they didn't force the hatching of the turtles which is cruel. 2. The beach is beautiful and they make you pick up litter before/after releasing turtles. 3. The guys who work there are really nice and got us coconuts from the trees by the beach. It was just the best early evening of my life

It  is  not what you  expect you would see in the US at Seaworld. Remember where you are in the world and everything is not like the USA. With that said, it is a nice little place trying to make a difference.  It is educational and  kids are able to hold a sea turtle. The hosts are really  nice and the cost is cheap. It is a small place and you can walk through in a matter of minutes. Like most things in Sri Lanka  it is what expectations you carry with you that can determine your experience.

Love the fact that you get to hold baby, and bigger, turtles! This place is worth the visit if you are a animallover like me! Watching how the sri lankan people takes care of these little creatures, melts my heart!

This is a place that rescues and hatch turtles. They buy and hatch turtleeggs from the market, where it’s sold as food. Some of the pounds for the big turtles seemed a little to small, and thats why they don’t get full score. It’s a small place, so you don’t need a lot of time to visit here. We used 30 minutes.

I'm sorry I just came away from this feeling far worse for the experience, we were rushed round and they were waiting for a tip longer than the tour took, I found this dirty and not an attraction at all. Good luck to anyone saving these lovely creatures but this place left me with the Henie jeebies

Visiting Unawatuna find time to visit turtle hatchery. Excursion will take maximum 30 minutes still the memories will be great. Interesting info about turtles; possibility to hold turtles; to feed and to see 1 day old turtle. Very nice experience.
Visited here after tsunami museum. Lovely to hold the baby turtles, and see how they are being helped

One of many great conservation projects along the coast. Rs 500 entry fee & an informative guide. Only takes a few minutes out of your day & can be visited together with the Tsunami museum & the Buddha monument.

They buy turtle eggs at high prices as locals tend to steal them from mounds and eat them for believed good properties. The eggs cost 6 rupees per egg, the brothers pay 20rupees per egg which is considered a high price. The tanks are small and the life of turtles who are kept there for education and the ones who have lost one of their limbs due to fishing net are kind of sad. Sacrificing some for the good of others i guess? Worth a visit, better than a so called elephant sanctuaries.

A simple place run by two brothers, doing their bit to take in eggs and hatch young as well as look after injured turtles. The entry is RS500, about £2.50 which goes into the running of the place. You can handle the small ones.

I loved our time visiting the turtle sanctuary! We got to hold and play with the turtles! So lovely ! They are doing brilliant work and I would defiantly recommend everyone to go and help their cause!
We all liked this place, especially our children. We couldnt join any turtle release but still it was a nice experience to come close to those turtles.
Bright explanation, supported also by princentuin school in Breda. Owner is dedicated and devoted to the animals

We spent about 45 minutes here . It’s well worth the visit . They explain some of the issues faced by the turtles in the area and their very practical solutions, without being a lecture . You can get up close to the turtles in their pools. The host is informative, knowledgeable and obviously passionate about what they are doing. Our kids loved it . Definitely worth checking out when in Hikkaduwa.

This is run by an individual with a sad history. Seems like the turtles are taken well care of. There were many kinds and we could pick up the baby turtles. Unfortunately not enough eggs had hatched to release them in the sea but we got to witness one come out of its egg. For 500 LKR, it's a worthwhile visit.

Great place to visit if you’re in the area! Nice to know your tourist dollar is also helping a cause. You get to see 1 day old turtle hatchlings the day before they are released. They also appreciate any donations you can make as they are self funded.

This is an excellent place to see how turtles are being rescued and being put back into the sea.  Foundation set up by local family.  Great place to visit, short lecture and you can hold baby turtles.  For once not a money making experience and you can see that a small entrance fee is very well used.
Just go here. For 500 rupees to see some baby turtles it is more than worth it! The staff are friendly and helpful, as are the turtles!

The turtles are so cute. This place is all about education and explaining the different turtles. They try and preserve each variety.  Visitors pay a small fee to enter which goes to looking after the turtles before they are released in the wild.  They also look after injured turtles. Visitors can touch the turtles also.

Took my two kids, 4 and 6 years, to this place to break the beach habit. Its a small hatchery with a cozy vibe. We got a good lecture about turtles and saw some lovely animals. The kids loved the place.

We were sceptical at first after reading some reviews about whether this was just a ‘tourist trap’ or genuine. After visiting and chatting to the owner and staff who work there it was clear that they really do care about these turtles and want to help them. The owner told us details about how long they stay there after hatching and when they get released into the ocean (not long at all) and the different steps he takes before releasing injured turtles back in the ocean. He told us that educating the next generation of Sri Lankan’s about turtles and how to look after them was something he was passionate about which was good. It’s true there are some big turtles there who are so badly injured (some missing 2 arms) that it is unlikely they will ever be released back into the ocean. It would just be nice if they had a bigger pool to swim in but obviously he can only work with what he’s got. Bare in mind this is not a fancy aquarium like we have in Europe but I believe the intention there is good and genuine so would visit.

The turtle hatchery is a great place to visit, and see turtles of various different types and sizes. You can never be too sure if places handling wild creatures are kind or cruel, but this hatchery seems to be doing a good thing, helping injured turtles learn to dive and feed before releasing them again, and providing a safe place for eggs to hatch and releasing the babies back into to sea. We did hold some of the smaller turtles, but I did feel guilty about everybody picking up every single turtle they saw so I decided just to take pictures rather than touching every single one. I’m not sure if they mind being handled or not but it’s probably quite stressful for them so try to keep it to a minimum.

Not so big place, but interesting to hear the staff tell about their work to save the turtles. They have different types of turtles, and both big and baby turtles. You also got to hold some turtles decided by the staff.

We went with my nephew who was 9 and he loved it as well as everyone else. Our guide talks you through the whole process from eggs hatching through to releasing turtle back to the wild. It was a heartwarming experience. Our guide was very passionate about education children so the next generation know how to treat the beautiful endangered species with respect. Let's hope it's not too late.

They do some great work in turtle conservation well worthy of support. The short talk/tour thay do is very informative and gives you an idea of the challenges that the turtle population face with people

I think it costs 500 rupees to visit this small hatchery. There were 1 day old turtles when we visited them and they were so cute. Also, you can see bigger turtles who have lost some of their fins and under rehabilitation. But the star of the show is the owner. He explained to us everything about what he is trying to achieve at this hatchery as well as provide education of these turtles. He looks after and feeds these turtles and will then release them into the wild once they are fully recovered or after they are big enough to survive on their own.

The best experience we've had in sri lanka! The owner teach the local and turist about the different turtles, their lives and how to save them. He helps handicapped turtles, which were hurt by fishing nets or boats, to learn how to survive in the ocean. Then release them back. Every day they release baby tutles back to the ocean. We wish you'll all go! The money is donation.

I've read some negative reviews and I'm a bit surprised by the criticism. Sri Lanka is a developing country. You can't drink the water from the tap, good trash collecting infrastructure doesn't exist and yet people seem to expect this to be a fancy aquarium and rescue center. It is sad to see the turtles who can't be rehabilitated swimming around the small concrete tanks and realize they will be there for decades. However, the alternative to this sanctuary is....drowning in the fisher men's nets.  At least here they have veterinary care and a place to go, even if it is less than ideal. The sanctuary also takes the recently laid turtle eggs out of the beach and keeps them in a secured area until the baby turtles hatch - if left of the beach most of the eggs/new hatchlings are killed by people and animals. They have a higher survival rate with the sanctuary than if left alone. By supporting this sanctuary you're helping increase the locals awareness of the importance of helping the turtles, and by visiting and donating to the sanctuary it allows them to (albeit slowly) better their facilities. It was a great educational opportunity for my kids.
A guide showed us the different pools with different turtles after a quick information session about the different species. It is quite a small place, but really cool to see their great effort

Rather disappointing. It is a collection of concrete ponds with various turtles. There is also a sand bed with eggs. The eggs are dug up and sold to the hatchery for a little more than they get from the restaurants. It is rather basic level in environmental terms.
8 concrete pools with all ages of turtles. 500 rupees pp so ok priced. Not the best guide but serviceable. I got my questions answered. Good for a 15 min visit.

We read some bad reviews regarding the state of the hatchery and questioning the living conditions of these turtles but we had to check it out. It is indeed sad that some of these handicapped turtles are required to live in small containers, but after talking with one of the caretakers they mentioned that with the money they earn, it is hard to provide them better living conditions. It makes sense for them to open it up to tourists for a source of income and they don't ask a lot (just 500 rupees) they can easily ask for much more but they have a box where you can provide them with a little extra. Obviously, they want to provide the turtles with better conditions, but after the tsunami they had to rebuild the compound. The current owner took it over from his sister who passed away during the tsunami who in turn took it over from her father. It's a family organisation trying to save what's left. If you want, you can even help them release new born baby turtles to the sea or if rehabilitated, help release the bigger ones.

Really interesting to see what effort is being put into helping injured Turtles to recover and return to the sea. A passion and devotion of the local family involved - within their means they are doing a lot - so much could be done to lift this exhibit and help visitors spend more time there, but money is no doubt the lack. it is important to visit and see and support but the visit only really takes a maximum of 20-30 minutes.
Not very impressed, no one there, bit of a one man show, nothing really to tell us what it was all about, tanks battered, not very clean, hurried us round, and then disappeared. big let down.
Finally, this people forces for donations. That disappointed me. But a nice place to visit. Various types of turtles available
These poor turtles are injured because of humans and I am happy some people care for them
Was great. Kids loved it. The amount of effort put in to protect and conserve the turtles is admirable.

A good place to gain knowledge on the topic. The staff here is doing much hard work to maintain the place and take care of the turtles. If you are travelling to Hikkaduwa, It's worth that you visit this place.
We visited the turtle hatchery yesterday and we learnt so much about these amazing ocean creatures. The tour was great to learn about marine life and how they take so much care of the sea turtles
We had luck to have guide about this place from its owner. It is very great work to save turtles. Do not miss your chance to tip this guys. We touched baby turtles.

It’s okay, probably not what I was expecting as it seemed to be getting sold everywhere. It’s a good cause as it helps wounded turtles etc. If you’re in hikkaduwa it’s worth a visit as it’s close but wouldn’t bother if you’re over say 20mins away, unless of course you’re a massive turtle enthusiast.

This turtle hatchery is a worthwhile stop in Hikkadua. The owner obviously cares greatly for the ongoing survival of turtles in the area, and the entry fee is your contribution to this. He described how they care for the turtle eggs before releasing back into the wild, as well as the rehabilitation of injured turtles that local fisherman bring in. The owner sadly lost much of his family in the tsunami, making the rebuilding of this hatchery even more meaningful. A donation box is on site.
An interesting place to visit and hear of the work being done to secure the future of sea turtles and the rescue and rehabilitation of injured turtles.
Interesting place to visit. Good to hear the story behind it and also to see the fantastic work they are doing.
Dropped in on the turtle sanctuary. Dont expect a long visit but it was a great look at a worthy project that is doing some great work. Def worth checking out while in Hikkaduwa

At the start I was a bit put off when I saw the massive turtles in the very small pools. But after having a closer look at them and the owner giving us a tour and explaining us the whole purpose it put it all in a much nicer light. Loads of the older and bigger turtles have lost one or even 2 legs. He is teaching them how to dive and swim with the nee circumstances and releasing them bank into the wild once they are able to dive for their own food. Furthermore he is helping turtles to hatch and releasing them into the sea. As eggs in the wild are taken by locals to eat with the believe of longer life's. I would usually be a rather critical person when it comes to zoo's and keeping animals in captivity but I believe this project has a good purpose.

My husband and I visited whilst stopping in Hikkaduwa. It's a small rescue centre/education centre. The owner explained he pays the local fishermen a premium rate when they find an injured turtle or turtle eggs so he can help rehabilitate them or help them to hatch so he can then release them back to the sea. There's a small entrance fee and a donation box - if you visit please give a donation as this man is really trying to make a difference. I've been lucky enough to see a government funded turtle hatchery in Borneo which is on a much bigger scale and shows that these organisations really do make a difference.

One should is it this hatchery - They have very old turtles and the guys are hospitable - They really take good care of the turtles and show you around. They have baby turtles - leather back and other breeds as well.

If they’re actually doing all the things they TELL you they are, then it’s worth paying the 500 rupees. There are some baby turtles, but mostly handicapped ones. Almost like visiting a turtle freak show. Generally worth a quick 10 minute stopover if you’re in the area.

They are doing important job. Eventough there was some handicaps, blind or without legs, who were lonely in small tanks. Is that then life worth of living... We see turtle babys who were only two hours old. Those were adorable!

500 rupees to visit for tourists? Seems unreasonable given this place should be supported by the government. We weren't given any sort of tour until a big group arrived as we were about to leave, and the tanks (concrete slabs filled with water) seemed small and sad for the turtles. He claims to release all these turtles and I hope that's true, otherwise I feel sorry for them spending Thier time here. I also question the practice of getting eggs from the beach, buying them off people is one thing (also encourages the practice!) But picking them up yourself rather than just letting them go?
The purpose of the visit was to experience these wonderful creatures.  It was totally worth it . Would come back again

The turtle hatchery looked genuine and we enjoyed holding the baby turtles. The turtles that are in captivity are handicapped which gives a positive feeling about their situation. We felt not obliged to give anything more then the entrance fee of 500 rps which felt good spent on the safe hatching of the baby turtles :) Worthwhile for a roadstop if your passing by!

This place is on the way from Colombo to Galle, It only takes 20-30minutes, but it is a must watch. They buy eggs from the fisherman at a price and I hub ate the eggs until they hatch and Once the turtles are ready they leave them at the sea, They also provide shelter to few turtles which have lost their fins. Good educative Place for kids

The turtle hatchery is another one of the to-do things on the road from Galle to Colombo. They conserve turtle eggs from various species that have been laid in nearby beaches across different times. When the eggs hatch, they keep the baby turtles for a few days before letting them free in the ocean. They also take care of some disabled turtles - ones without limbs or those who have been badly injured somehow. You can take a picture with a turtle and if you are lucky enough you can also set free one of the baby turtles into the ocean.

Good initiative to help the turtles reach their habitat. The owner takes care of the disabled turtles (missing limbs) found ashore, helps them learn survive in the tanks and then releases them back once sure of regaining their ability to swim and find their food. The baby turtles are extremely cute, kids love handling them. Entrance fee is LKR 500 per adult.

We went to the hatchery today and spent about an hour with the turtles. They collect turtle eggs that would otherwise be sold to locals, keep them until they hatch then release most of them back into the wild. They also look after injured turtles and try to rehabilitate them until they are able to go back to the sea. There was some information on boards and the owner gave us a brief talk. Seeing the turtles was amazing up close although the size of the tanks for the large turtles was a bit small. They let you handle the little turtles which I wasn't sure about never having been allowed at other turtle rescue centres. It's a small place and perhaps not the most professional but interesting and anything that can be done to protect them is a plus!!

These hatcheries charge 500 srilankan rupees but cant say how much work they talk about and how much they do. the place isn't that well kept. If you have time then you can pay a visit here, please do, you only need 30 minutes here, think that ticket price is the charity money you are giving to save these turtles. hope these hatcheries are actually using this money to save turtles.
Not a  pleasant experience . Pay fisherman for turtle eggs which they then hatch and release but seems to be a money making exercise. There are quite a few hatcheries probably far too many

We visited this turtle hatchery but I was disappointed mainly because of our guide. He took us round every tank and explained everything at break neck speed, all the time looking at his watch.
